DSA 2050 · Option 06 · Applied Data Science Methodology

Water Supply Reliability Monitoring

Which NYCHA developments show recurring disruption or abnormal consumption, and which simply are not being read?

1 HCF = 748 gallons = 2,832 litres HCF = hundred cubic feet, the unit on the water bill Use is reported as gallons per apartment per day Money is in US dollars
Units and terms used throughout this dashboard
HCFHundred cubic feet, the unit New York bills water in. One HCF is 748 US gallons (about 2,832 litres). Raw bills arrive in HCF; everything a person reads here is converted to gallons.
HCF per dayA bill's water divided by the days it covers, so a 45-day bill and a 28-day bill compare fairly.
Gallons per
apartment per day		The headline measure. A typical value is about 203. A figure near zero means the meters are not covering the homes, not that nobody is using water.
DevelopmentOne public-housing estate: a named group of apartment buildings managed together, identified by a TDS number. This is the zone the decision question asks about. 104 of them here.
Development-monthOne development in one month: the unit of analysis, and what one row of data describes. 9,609 in total.
Bill monthThe month a bill is billed under. A billing period does not line up exactly with a calendar month, so timing is accurate to within a billing period, not to a day.
MeterThe device on the incoming pipe that counts water passing through it. It measures a pipe, not a place.
Metering coveragewhole: meters cover the residential buildings, so per-apartment use is meaningful (70 developments). partial: only a shop or community-centre meter, so per-apartment use is meaningless and these are excluded from consumption analysis (29). unknown: too few real readings to tell.
Measurement gapA month not really measured: estimated (the company guessed from past use), zero_read (the meter reported nothing), or missing_bill (no bill at all).
Expected useWhat the model predicts a development should use this month, based mostly on what it used last month.
zHow far actual use sits from expected, measured in that development's own typical surprise. z = 4 is four times its normal wobble. The bars in |z| mean direction is ignored: too much water may be a leak, too little a supply failure.
LiftHow much more often a flag lands on a development residents were also complaining about, versus chance. Lift 3.4 = 3.4 times more often.
ChargesMoney on the bill, in US dollars. Water used and money charged are not the same thing, because rates change over time.

The decision this supports

Fix the meter
Readings keep going missing or are estimated, so consumption cannot be judged at all.
Inspect for leaks
Use is repeatedly far from what this development normally uses.
Monitor
Nothing recurring: no crew needed this month.

Key findings

Citywide picture over time

How to read it: the top line is how much water a typical apartment uses per day, one point per month. The bottom orange band is how many developments were not properly read that month. When the orange rises and the line dips together, the fall in water is not real; it is fewer meters being read.

Read the two panels together: a dip in use that lines up with a spike in gaps is a measurement artefact, not a real fall in consumption.

Measurement gaps: the biggest reliability problem

Real reads vs measurement gaps, by year

How to read it: each bar is one year, split by what kind of month it was. The dark graphite blue is a real meter reading; everything else is a gap. That blue band shrinking year by year is the central finding of the project.

Labels in the current selection

Why this matters
An estimated bill is a carried-forward guess, not a measurement: estimated months change 2.7% from month to month against 6.8% for real reads. A leak during an estimated month is invisible.

Developments with the most gap months

How to read it: the 20 developments whose meters are read least often. A long bar means most of that development's bills were guessed rather than measured, so nobody really knows what it is using. First places to send a meter technician.

Consumption, boroughs and uncertainty

How to read it: how common each level of water use is. Most months sit in the middle hump; thin tails are the unusual months. The axis is squeezed (log scale) so rare extremes stay visible.

By borough

How to read it: each box covers the middle half of that borough's months, with a line at the typical value. Boxes that overlap heavily mean the boroughs are not really different.

Cluster-bootstrap 95% confidence intervals

Use per apartment

Gap rate

The intervals overlap, so no borough is clearly different. Bronx minus Queens is +100 gal/apt/day with a 95% CI of [-7, 197], which includes 0. Months of one development are correlated, so the bootstrap resamples whole developments, not rows.

Season and weather

Seasonal pattern

How to read it: all the Januarys together, all the Februarys together, and so on. A flat row means the time of year barely matters.

How to read it: each dot is one month: temperature across, water use up. A shapeless cloud means hot months are no thirstier than cold ones, so weather does not help predict this, which is why the model does not lean on it.

Expected use, then two decision rules

Layer 1 predicts each development's expected use for the month. Layer 2 flags months far from expected. Split by time, never shuffled: train to Dec 2021, validate 2022, test Jan 2023 – May 2025.

Accuracy (MAE on the log scale, lower is better)

The candidate had the lowest validation error, so it was used for flagging. On test it is 37% more accurate than seasonal naive (target was 10%), but only 1.5% better than persistence. Comparing with the last actual reading is nearly as good and far simpler.

Rule A (citywide band) vs Rule B (own history)

One thing to notice: this table compares the two rules at |z| > 3, the comparison threshold, not the operating one. The threshold actually chosen, on the 2022 validation year and for crew capacity, is |z| > 4.5, which flags 6.0% of months on the test period. Comparing the rules and setting the operating point are deliberately separate decisions.

Sensitivity: what the threshold choice costs

How to read it: every dot is one possible threshold. Right = more months flagged = more work. Up = flags land on genuinely troubled developments more often. The best settings sit high and to the left.

Why gaps are labelled before flagging

Zero reads are flagged about three times as often as real reads: false alarms unless recognised as gaps. Estimated months look normal, so a real problem during one is invisible.

Priority list: the answer to the decision question

Two different reliability problems

How to read it: each circle is one development, sized by how many apartments it has. Far right = its meters keep going unread. High up = its water use keeps coming out strange. Colour is the action the rules recommend.

Move the sliders in the sidebar to see the trade-off: a lower threshold flags more months (more work, more false alarms), a higher one flags fewer (more missed problems). The report's operating threshold is 4.5, chosen on the 2022 validation year, never on the test period.

Look at one development

How to read it: the solid line is what this development actually used. The dashed orange line is what the model expected. Dot colour says whether the month was really measured or only guessed. An orange triangle marks a month far enough from expected to be worth a visit.

Where the data comes from

Only aggregated 311 counts were downloaded and dataset A holds no tenant information, so no personal data enters the repository. Raw files are kept out of GitHub and can be rebuilt with python src/download_data.py.

Cleaning rules C1–C9

Data-quality audit

The documented SQL join (q07)

SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM bills_clean)                 AS rows_before_join,
       COUNT(*)                                           AS rows_after_left_join,
       SUM(CASE WHEN d.tds IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)     AS unmatched_rows
FROM   bills_clean AS b
LEFT JOIN developments AS d ON d.tds = b.tds;
28,635 rows before and after the LEFT JOIN, with no fan-out. 225 rows (0.79%) from 2 developments did not match the 2025 Data Book. All 13 queries and the two monthly views are in sql/queries.sql.
